title: Why performance resists preservation (rev)
content: A novel outlives its author because the marks on the page hold all that the work needs. A symphony outlives its composer because notation keeps the links among pitches and lengths that make up the piece. Dance has no such safety. What a dancer does exists only while she does it, and the film that remains stands to the event roughly as a photo of a meal stands to its taste. This gap reaches well beyond the archive. Because a performance cannot be stored, it cannot be bought, sold, or piled up, and so it sits oddly inside museums built around things they own. A museum can buy an object; it cannot buy an afternoon. Curators have answered by buying the score rather than the event, treating the maker's notes as the lasting work and each staging as one case of it. Yet this answer smuggles in the very claim it meant to avoid, since it moves the work into a durable text and thus denies that the passing encounter was the point. Some hold that the loss is the meaning. On their view a performance attacks the buying and selling of art just by leaving nothing behind, and any attempt to keep it betrays it. Others reply that this makes a virtue of neglect and writes off whole traditions, above all those of people whose practice was never set down. The quarrel is not merely academic, because it decides which stories can be told. Where the record is dismissed as false, the record thins, and later readers inherit an account built from whatever happened to last. Loss, then, is never neutral. It spreads forgetting unevenly, along the same lines as who had time, money, and a camera.

title: Improvisation and the myth of spontaneity (rev)
content: Listeners often treat improvisation as playing without any plan, as though the player had made up each note on the spot. Musicians who improvise tell a different story. They speak of a stock of phrases built up over years, of runs drilled until the hand finds them without thought, and of chord shapes so well learned that the player can attend to the arc of a solo rather than to the fingers. On this account freedom is not the opposite of practice but its fruit, since only long practice makes fast choice possible. The point matters because the common picture hands improvisation to instinct and writing to labour, and that split shapes how whole traditions are ranked. Music passed on by ear rather than by score has often been called natural, and the word, though meant as praise, denies those players the credit given to written music for craft and thought. What sounds easy is thus mistaken for what took no work. Studies of skill back the players rather than the listeners. Good improvisers lean on stored patterns much as chess masters do when they read a board, and their ease comes from recall rather than from invention. The freedom an audience hears is real, but it is freedom inside a frame that rules out most moves in advance and leaves a small set to choose among. Seeing this does not shrink the feat. It puts the feat where players have always put it, in the long build-up of means that lets a choice be made in the space of one beat, and it strips away the faint scorn that follows whenever skill is renamed instinct.

title: Taste, distinction, and the shape of liking (rev)
content: What we like in music, food, and furniture feels deeply our own, and people defend such likes as marks of who they are. Studies in sociology muddy this picture without quite refuting it. Large surveys find that taste tracks schooling and upbringing closely, and that the link holds even when income is held steady, which hints that what people enjoy is tied to how they were formed rather than to what they can pay for. The path proposed is one of habit rather than choice. Children pick up ways of paying attention from the homes they grow up in, learning which things repay a long look and which talk counts as serious, and these habits later show up as likes that seem to come from nowhere. Because they are picked up early and go unremarked, they feel natural, and their social root stays hidden above all from those who hold them. Critics say this explains too much. If every liking marks a place in a social order, then the account cannot tell a judgment reached by long attention from one soaked up without thought, and it leaves no room for anyone to change their mind on the merits. Its defenders reply that the account maps tendencies rather than fates, and that showing where a taste came from does not settle whether it is sound. The quarrel is unsettled, yet it leaves one thing standing. Whatever else taste may be, it is not free of history, and the ease with which people report their likes is a poor guide to where those likes began.
